title: Latino identity remains a source of belonging and linked fate while also being experienced as a barrier, with meaning shifting across generations
source_unit: Pew Research Center, U.S. Hispanics Are Divided on Whether Their Identity Helps or Hurts Them in America
geography: United States; Hispanic/Latino adults by nativity, immigrant generation, language and political affiliation

observations.period: October 6-16, 2025 survey; identity importance and perceived effect on getting ahead

denominator.unit: U.S. Latino adults in Pew National Survey of Latinos

identity_importance.unit: per cent saying being Hispanic is extremely or very important to how they think about themselves

identity_helps.unit: per cent saying being Hispanic helps their ability to get ahead in America a lot or a little

identity_hurts.unit: per cent saying being Hispanic hurts their ability to get ahead a lot or a little

identity_neither.unit: per cent saying being Hispanic neither helps nor hurts their ability to get ahead

identity_meaning_split.value: Identity can be central to self-understanding while being interpreted as a source of connection or discrimination and reduced opportunity.

observations.method: Nationally representative bilingual survey conducted online and by live telephone interview, recruited through national random address sampling and weighted to U.S. adult population benchmarks.
observations.uncertainty: Perceptions of identity’s effect on advancement do not measure labor-market discrimination, institutional treatment or actual mobility; responses may vary with political context and question framing.
observations.subgroup: U.S. Hispanic adults by identity importance, nativity, immigrant generation, political affiliation and experiences of advantage or exclusion.
observations.counterinterpretation: The gap between identity importance and perceived advantage may reflect a distinction between cultural belonging and access to institutions, not a rejection of identity.

observations.period: October 2025 survey; reported identity-related discrimination and support

denominator.unit: U.S. Latino adults; Spanish-speaking question restricted where noted

identity_discrimination.unit: per cent personally experiencing discrimination or unfair treatment by someone who is not Hispanic because of Hispanic background in prior 12 months

spanish_criticism.unit: per cent of relevant respondents criticized for speaking Spanish in public

go_back_remark.unit: per cent reporting being told to go back to their home country

offensive_names.unit: per cent reporting offensive names because they are Hispanic

identity_support.unit: per cent saying someone expressed support for them because they are Hispanic

observations.method: Survey battery on identity-related experiences in the previous year, with separate wording and denominator for speaking-Spanish question.
observations.uncertainty: The battery is not exhaustive; self-reported incidents do not identify perpetrators, institutional remedies, frequency or effects on employment, health or political participation.
observations.subgroup: Hispanic adults, including Spanish speakers and respondents reporting discrimination, hostility or identity-based support.
observations.counterinterpretation: The coexistence of support and discrimination points to an uneven social environment rather than one uniformly hostile or welcoming experience.

observations.period: October 2025 survey; identity importance and self-labels across immigrant generations

denominator.unit: U.S. Hispanic adults, including immigrants, second-generation and third-or-higher-generation adults

identity_importance_immigrants.unit: per cent of Hispanic immigrants saying being Latino is extremely or very important to identity

american_only_label.value: 5% of immigrants, 22% of second-generation and 40% of third-or-higher-generation Hispanics most often refer to themselves as American alone.

heritage_label.value: 67% of immigrants, 49% of second-generation and 34% of third-or-higher-generation Hispanics most often use labels including country of origin or heritage.

observations.method: Weighted survey comparison of identity importance, heritage and national self-labels across nativity and immigrant generations.
observations.uncertainty: Generational comparisons are cross-sectional and do not track the same families over time; age, cohort, language, place and changing racial categories may contribute to differences.
observations.subgroup: Hispanic immigrants, second-generation Hispanics and third-or-higher-generation Hispanics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Greater use of ‘American’ does not necessarily mean loss of Latino belonging; people may hold national, pan-ethnic and origin identities simultaneously.

observations.period: October 2025 survey; linked fate, immigrant connection and collective responsibility

denominator.unit: U.S. Hispanic adults in Pew National Survey of Latinos

linked_to_other_hispanics.value: 65% of immigrants, 67% of second-generation and 55% of third-or-higher-generation Hispanics say what happens to other Hispanics affects their own lives a great deal or fair amount.

immigrant_legal_link.unit: per cent of Hispanic immigrants saying what happens to Latino immigrants living legally in the country affects their lives a great deal or fair amount

immigrant_unauthorized_link.unit: per cent of Hispanic immigrants saying what happens to Latino immigrants living illegally affects their lives a great deal or fair amount

look_out_responsibility.value: 38% of immigrants and second-generation Hispanics and 29% of third-or-higher-generation Hispanics say they feel a responsibility to look out for other Hispanics extremely or very often.

observations.method: Survey measures of perceived connection to other Hispanics, immigrant groups and collective responsibility across immigrant generations.
observations.uncertainty: Perceived linked fate is not observed mutual aid, political mobilization or resource transfer; the wording distinguishes connection from responsibility and action.
observations.subgroup: Hispanic immigrants, U.S.-born second-generation and third-or-higher-generation adults, and views of legal and unauthorized immigrants.
observations.counterinterpretation: People can perceive common exposure or linked outcomes without adopting a pan-ethnic identity or engaging in collective action; low reported responsibility does not imply indifference.

related_sources.claim: Official Pew identity report page with generational, linked-fate and self-label findings.
Related Pew American Dream source connecting identity to household security and intergenerational mobility.

boundary: This record adds an identity-and-belonging layer: Latino identity can be central to self-understanding and linked fate while also being experienced as discrimination or a barrier to advancement; meanings shift across immigrant generations without implying a simple assimilation or disappearance of belonging. It is representative survey evidence, not an administrative discrimination census, longitudinal identity trajectory, causal political behavior study or measure of actual mobility.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Pew report PDF and identity pages were reviewed for survey scope, identity importance, advantage and disadvantage, discrimination experiences, language, generational labels, linked fate and collective responsibility boundaries.
